question: What gives a very dark roast most of its harsh, lingering bitterness?
answer: Breakdown products of chlorogenic acids. Green beans are rich in these acids; roasting turns them first into lactones with a sharp bitterness, then, in dark roasts, into phenylindanes with a harsher, lingering one. Caffeine supplies only a small share of coffee's bitterness, which is why a decaffeinated dark roast still tastes bitter.
move: The best-known suspect is not always the one doing most of the work.
trap: Blaming caffeine, the one bitter molecule everyone has heard of.
reference: Blumberg, Frank & Hofmann, Quantitative studies on the influence of the bean roasting parameters and hot water percolation on the concentrations of bitter compounds in coffee brew, Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry, 2010
